title: On Subjective Uncertainty Quantification and Calibration in Natural Language Generation
abstract: Applications of large language models often involve the generation of free-form responses, in which case uncertainty quantification becomes challenging. This is due to the need to identify task-specific uncertainties (e.g., about the semantics) which appears difficult to define in general cases. This work addresses these challenges from a perspective of Bayesian decision theory, starting from the assumption that our utility is characterized by a similarity measure that compares a generated response with a hypothetical true response. We discuss how this assumption enables principled quantification of the model's subjective uncertainty and its calibration. We further derive a measure for epistemic uncertainty, based on a missing data perspective and its characterization as an excess risk. The proposed methods can be applied to black-box language models. We illustrate the methods on question answering and machine translation tasks. Our experiments provide a principled evaluation of task-specific calibration, and demonstrate that epistemic uncertainty offers a promising deferral strategy for efficient data acquisition in in-context learning.

claims.text: Subjective uncertainty in natural language generation can be quantified as the Bayes risk based on a similarity-characterized utility function.
Instruction tuning causes a much smaller deterioration in task-specific calibration than in token-level probability calibration across question answering benchmarks.
Probabilistic uncertainty quantification achieves lower Expected Calibration Error than prompt-based confidence elicitation methods across question answering datasets.
Epistemic uncertainty-based deferral in many-shot in-context learning achieves statistically significant improvements in AUC-DF over random selection for low-resource machine translation.
Selective prediction performance based on task-specific uncertainty is approximately unchanged or improved following instruction tuning.
Total uncertainty quantification does not consistently outperform random deferral when predictive uncertainty is irreducible.

limitations.text: Semantic equivalence estimation relies on machine learning classifiers that produce imprecise estimates failing to guarantee formal equivalence relations.
Standard token-level entropy conflates task-irrelevant variations, such as response style and fact selection, with actual task performance uncertainty.
The proposed epistemic uncertainty deferral strategy shows reduced efficacy when applied to severely miscalibrated base language models such as gemini-1.5-pro.
The epistemic uncertainty formula uses a finite number of missing observations N, which acts as a lower bound rather than exact quantification of total theoretical epistemic uncertainty.

future_work.text: Extend the decision-theoretic epistemic uncertainty framework beyond in-context learning to interactive settings involving user clarifying questions or external datastore queries.
Develop instruction-tuning and fine-tuning methodologies specifically optimized for improving task-specific probabilistic calibration in language models.

methodologies.name: Minimum Bayes Risk Task-Specific Calibration Evaluation
methodologies.description: Measures task-specific expected calibration error by evaluating expected loss under an explicit utility measure using Monte Carlo sampling and histogram binning.
conditions: gpt-4o-mini used as judge model for semantic similarity utility
10 Monte Carlo generation samples per query

methodologies.name: Missing-Data Epistemic Uncertainty Estimation in ICL
methodologies.description: Quantifies reducible epistemic uncertainty in in-context learning as the excess risk between predictions made with and without synthetic model-generated demonstration pairs.
conditions: 4 base in-context demonstrations vs 128 many-shot demonstrations
5 synthetic demonstration sequences with 8 output samples per sequence
